accuracy.evidence: Format checked against the WSDC Rules (August 2026 edition, parts 5, 11 and 13) and Debate England's World Schools guide: two teams of three; each speaker speaks once; proposition first, alternating; 8-minute substantive speeches and 4-minute replies (5.4); POIs only between the 1st and 7th minute (13.1), about 15 seconds, accepted or declined; reply by the 1st or 2nd speaker, never the 3rd (11.2), opposition reply first and proposition last (11.3); no new part of the case in a reply, but a new example for an existing argument is allowed (11.4-11.5); sides are allocated. The adult text says other formats use other timings. The motion and its arguments are practice material, not factual claims. Numeric answers a-2 (a 5-8), 56+a (6 × 8 + 2 × 4 = 56), a*15 and a*2 checked at the corners.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets slips teachers and debate coaches report in KS3 debating: refusing or half-arguing an allocated side (Motion predict 'Argue it badly or refuse', challenge 'side', m2); opposition opening or getting the last word (Speaking order predict, order feedback 'The proposition always opens' and 'Replies flip', challenge 'order', m3, p5); straw-man rebuttal (rebuttal options, MSG.straw, challenge 'straw', m6, sorter); attacking the person (MSG.person, challenge 'person', p3); answering with an unrelated point (MSG.off); POIs in protected time or in replies (POI predict, first, last and reply feedback, challenge 'poi', m7); saving a new argument for the reply (reply-plan check, MSG.newArg, challenge 'newarg', m4), while knowing a new example is allowed (MSG.example).

lab_distinct.evidence: flagdebate is built on debate mechanics no other lab has: a motion with argument cards dragged onto proposition and opposition zones, a World Schools running order of eight speeches with the reply flip, rebuttal choices that separate a fair summary from straw men, personal attacks and off-topic answers, a minute-by-minute grid of an 8-minute speech and a 4-minute reply where POIs are allowed or protected, and a reply-speech plan that must keep every clash and the new example but drop the new argument. The persuasive writing and opinion labs build a written argument or an 'I think ... because' sentence; none has sides, speaking order, POIs or reply rules. The lab_distinct gate measures it under 30% against every flagship lab.

lab_teaches.evidence: The learner finds each rule by acting on it: sorting cards shows that each argument helps one side whatever the learner thinks; tapping speeches in order and being stopped at the reply flip teaches who opens and closes; choosing between replies to three real points shows what makes rebuttal fair; tapping minutes reveals that only minutes 2-7 of a main speech accept POIs and replies accept none; ticking notes in or out and checking the plan shows that a reply keeps the clashes and an extra example but no new argument.

predictions.evidence: Four predictions, each with a tempting wrong option that the lab then corrects: 'Argue it badly or refuse' (cards must go to the side they help, not the side you like); 'The opposition, answering everything' gets the last word (the order ends with the proposition reply); 'Show the speaker is not very clever' (the personal-attack reply is rejected with feedback); 'Yes, at any time' for POIs in the first minute (minute 1 is rejected as protected). A.reveal confirms or corrects each prediction when the task is done.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Seven challenge questions rotate answer order; every wrong option has a named slip: 'motion' (the motion is the statement debated), 'order' (proposition opens, replies flip), 'poi' (only between the 1st and 7th minute), 'straw' (twisting their point), 'person' (attacking the speaker), 'newarg' (no new argument in a reply), 'side' (sides are given). In-lab mistakes also get specific messages: which side a card helps and why, who should speak next, why each wrong rebuttal fails, which protected minute was tapped, and which reply-plan note breaks the rules.

readability.evidence: Kid explanation Flesch-Kincaid grade 3.7 and adult 5.7, inside the learner limits (6.5 and 9.5). Kid paragraphs define each term in plain words (motion, proposition, opposition, rebuttal, straw man, point of information) in short sentences. Lab banners are one short instruction; feedback lines fit in four lines at 390 px.

no_filler.evidence: Each kid paragraph carries one rule set (motion and sides, order and timing, rebuttal, POIs and the reply); adult paragraphs give curriculum link and key words, the sourced format rules, common mistakes, and what the lab does. No filler phrases (content gate passed). The family tip is a concrete dinner-table mini debate with a coin toss for sides.

mobile.evidence: Checked on 390 px screenshots in light and dark themes before, during and after each task: the motion and argument card with two side zones, the 8 slots and 8 speech cards in two columns, the point and three reply cards above the drop box, the 8-minute and 4-minute grids, and the five reply notes with IN/OUT tags and the check button all fit without clipping. The argument card was enlarged and the finished rebuttal step now lists the three fair replies after the first screenshots.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas action has a button: proposition or opposition, each speech by name, Reply 1-3 with the full reply text in its aria-label, every minute of both speeches, put in or leave out each note, and Check my reply. The canvas aria-label updates after every action and c.say announces it. The browser gate's axe run (WCAG 2.1 AA) is clean in both themes on desktop and iPhone 13, with no console errors.

sources: World Schools Debating Championships, WSDC Rules (August 2026 edition), parts 5 (format and timing), 11 (reply speeches) and 13 (points of information)
Debate England, Resources for World Schools (speech roles, POIs between the 1st and 7th minute, no new material in replies)
WSDC Speaker Training notes (reply order, no new part of the case in a reply)
DfE (2013) English programmes of study: key stage 3, spoken English ('participating in formal debates and structured discussions, summarising and/or building on what has been said')
